newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Hardliners say Plavsic endangers Serb territory.
newsitem.headline: Hardliners say Plavsic endangers Serb territory.

text.p: Hardline foes of Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, in a scathing attack that raised tensions between feuding Serb leaders, accused her on Sunday of jeopardising the security of Serb territory.
Hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic launched the attack through official media after crisis talks announced earlier failed to materialise.

The Bosnian Serb SRNA news agency, under the strict control of Karadzic loyalists, said it had obtained a letter from the army commander demanding Plavsic consult the military "before taking any further decision in this situation".
Western envoys expressed serious doubts about the authenticity of the letter as army generals, in a statement issued three days ago, had vowed to stay out of the confrontation.

The said the report, combined with moves to strip Plavsic of defence powers and rewrite laws to enable her recall, indicated that Karadzic and his associates were preparing the ground for her removal.

Plavsic, who has gained international support in her battle with Karadzic's allies, has dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly and called for elections on September 1. But the hardliners have ignored her decision.

The letter carried by SRNA said Plavsic's order to dissolve parliament was "hasty" and had brought Bosnia's Serb entity "to the brink of ruin". The report alleged that the Moslem-Croat federation military was mobilising as a result.
There was no immediate response from Plavsic in the northwest town of Banja Luka, where nervous police who have sided with her are guarding the presidential offices.

Momcilo Krasjinik, a key Karadzic ally and the Serb member of the Bosnian collective presidency, had said he would hold talks with Plavsic on Sunday to resolve the conflict. But the meeting never took place.
Aides to Plavsic said the venue and agenda were never agreed. Political sources said Plavsic was reluctant to meet her rival outside Banja Luka out of fear for her safety.
Banja Luka, the largest town in Bosnia's Serb entity, has become Plavsic's power base but hardliners are believed to control the police force elsewhere.
The NATO-led peace force has stepped up patrols in and around Banja Luka to prevent a possible clash between Plavsic's supporters, which include military police, and Karadzic's security units.
Plavsic's opponents accused NATO of ordering British soldiers to help guard her building last week.
Army chief General Pero Colic arrived at the presidential offices on Sunday but local media said it was unclear if Plavsic received him.
Colic was appointed commander last year after Karadzic's party purged the army of senior officers who had viewed the civilian leadership as corrupt war profiteers.
Plavsic's detailed charges of high-level corruption have struck a chord among ordinary Serbs, especially in Banja Luka. Demonstrations in her support drew big crowds over the weekend.
A scheduled rally in the eastern town of Bijeljina on Sunday was cancelled without explanation, apparently a sign that tensions were mounting in the stand-off.
Although Plavsic is a nationalist ideologue, mediators say she has shown a willingness to cooperate with the Dayton peace accords to obtain reconstruction aid and investment for Serb territory.
Karadzic, twice indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, reluctantly stepped down from office last year but continues to wield influence in a bid to block the Dayton treaty.
